# Solution-design architecture brief (T001 draft)

**Status:** proposed architecture, not an implementation or the final solution-design contract. This brief is limited to the small synthetic password-reset application; no deployment, deployment workflow, or production-readiness claim is proposed.

## Components and boundaries

1. **Flask application factory and server-rendered Jinja views** (Python 3.12): routes for sign-in, reset request, neutral confirmation, new password, unusable link, and completion. Templates reuse labels, keyboard-operable controls, field-associated errors, focus/status announcements and a simple responsive card. Only the white canvas, centered outlined card, bold “Sign in”, “Email address” and “Password” labels, `name@example.com` hint, masked `********` example, blue underlined “Forgot password?” beneath the password field, dark full-width “Sign in” button, and gray “No account? Contact your administrator.” beneath it are observed. Their behavior, placeholder semantics, dimensions, breakpoints, other pages and accessibility properties are **design proposals**, not observed image facts. [Wireframe; Story]
2. **Recovery service with an injectable UTC clock and one synchronized in-memory store:** synthetic account IDs/email keys and password hashes; rolling request timestamps keyed by normalized address (including nonexistent addresses); reset records indexed by a digest of opaque tokens with account ID, issue/expiry time and consumed state; per-account session version. Hold one store lock for request accounting/issuance and for reset validation/commit to prevent oversubscription or token replay under concurrent requests. Provide a test-isolated store per application instance and clock-controlled fixtures. [Story; Recovery standard]
3. **In-memory outbox and owner-notification sink:** accepted requests for existing synthetic accounts place a reset URL in an owner-directed test-inspectable outbox; never return that URL on the public request page. A **separate** owner-notification record is appended for every successful change. No SMTP, external delivery, real accounts or actual owner contact is implied. [Story; Recovery standard]
4. **Session guard:** a signed Flask session cookie carries synthetic account ID and the version observed when a minimal demonstrator sign-in succeeds. Every authenticated route checks the current account version in the store. A completed reset increments it, rendering **all** previously issued cookies for that account unauthenticated, including the resetter's current session; clear a stale cookie at the next guarded response. The button's behavior is a chosen demonstration mechanism, not a wireframe inference or a complete authentication policy. [Wireframe; Recovery standard]

The trust boundary is browser ⇄ Flask routes ⇄ process-local services/store/sinks; the token in a URL is a bearer secret, while account existence, password hashes, rate counters and notification records remain server-side. The store and sink share one process; no database, migration or external event bus is within scope. Initial synthetic fixtures are loaded at startup/test setup; process restart loses request history, links, sessions' backing versions and notifications. Persistent migrations and multi-worker consistency are **production follow-up concerns**, not deliverables. [Story]

## Route and data contracts (proposed)

| Route | Request / response and side effects |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /` | Render sign-in card with literal observed copy and an `href` to `/forgot-password`; examples are hints, not prefilled secrets. |
| `POST /sign-in` | Accept labeled email/password fields for **synthetic** credentials only; on a match, set `(account_id, session_version)` in a signed cookie and redirect to a demonstrator authenticated view; invalid credentials get generic, field-associated feedback. This minimal authentication choice exists to exercise multiple sessions, not to specify real-world login policy. |
| `GET /forgot-password` | Render proposed account-address form and validation/accessibility affordances. |
| `POST /forgot-password` | For a syntactically acceptable address, normalize and apply the private rolling-hour counter, issue an owner-directed link **only** for an existing account below the limit, and always return the **same** neutral `303` redirect to `/reset-requested`. Existing, nonexistent, under-limit and throttled submissions share status, `Location`, public headers and confirmation body; no throttling banner, account echo, token, or account-derived cookie/flash value. Apply the same private accounting to nonexistent normalized identifiers to avoid a visible distinction. Empty/malformed addresses get the same form-validation response irrespective of existence. |
| `GET /reset-requested` | Static neutral confirmation (“If an account matches, check its reset instructions”) and return-to-sign-in link; no assertion that a link was sent. |
| `GET /reset/<token>` | Digest-lookup the opaque token; only an unused token with `now < issued_at + 30 minutes` reaches the new-password form. An unknown, used or expired token reaches a non-success retry page, without changing state. |
| `POST /reset/<token>` | CSRF-check, validate the proposed minimal password input, then **recheck** token existence, unused status and expiry under the store lock at commit time. A valid attempt updates the synthetic password hash, consumes the token, increments the account's session version and appends one owner-notification record for that success; only then `303` to `/reset-complete`. Used/expired/unknown attempts never change password, version or notifications and render a retry path, never a success claim. |
| `GET /reset-complete` | Proposed generic success page with link to sign-in; no token or account details. Authenticated demo routes require the version guard on **every** request. |

Transport is server-rendered HTML with standard form POSTs, not a JSON API. A valid email request uses Post/Redirect/Get; the redirect and destination must be static across account and limit states. If per-client CSRF state is used, it must be created independently of account lookup and cannot alter an otherwise equivalent response based on account existence. Do not put tokens in public request responses, session cookies, analytics, third-party assets or ordinary logs. Password values never appear in redirects or log entries. [Story; Recovery standard; Wireframe]

**Time, limits and token invariants.** Normalize synthetic addresses consistently (e.g. trim and case-fold the fixture's ASCII emails). At a request time `t`, remove timestamps `<= t - 3600 seconds`; honor the next existing-account issuance iff fewer than five timestamps remain, then record `t`. The sixth attempt before the oldest timestamp leaves the rolling window produces **no** further reset link but the same public response; at exactly one hour the old timestamp is outside the window. Nonexistent normalized keys use the same private counter policy without issuing a link. Generate a cryptographically random, URL-safe bearer token (e.g. 32 random bytes), store only its SHA-256 digest in the reset-record index, and place the URL in the process-local test outbox. Issue time is an injected timezone-aware UTC instant and expiration is exactly `issued_at + 30 minutes`: `now < expires_at` is valid, and `now >= expires_at` is invalid, **including equality**. GET never consumes; POST rechecks and consumes under the lock. Use a suitable framework password hasher, not reversible/plaintext storage. [Recovery standard; Story]

**Commit and failure semantics.** The in-memory store and owner sink must cooperate on a single synchronized success operation: validate and prepare the notification, mutate password/token/session version, and append exactly one notification before advertising success; if that in-process operation fails, do not claim completion and avoid a partial successful change without the notification (restore prior state or commit a prepared unit). A second POST, including concurrent submissions, sees the consumed token and cannot create a second success/notification. This is **process-local consistency only**, not durable transactions or guaranteed delivery after crashes. A GET view can be valid and a later POST can fail at the boundary; the commit-time clock decides. [Recovery standard; Story]

## Security, reliability, observability and operational limits

- CSRF-protect all state-changing forms; use framework output escaping and meaningful labels/errors; set `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` session cookie, `Secure` when served over HTTPS; never confuse a signed client-side cookie with server-side session revocation without checking the account version. Keep demonstrator secrets out of source; local-only configuration is not a production key-management plan. [Story; Recovery standard]
- Reset-token pages and responses use `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`; avoid third-party content on token pages, strip token path segments from request/error logs, and avoid reflecting submitted addresses. Internal metrics may count request attempts, honored issuances, throttles, successful resets, invalid/replayed/expired attempts and notification records **without** recording emails, raw tokens or passwords. Public status/copy must not vary with account existence; timing equality across paths is not proved by a static response and needs production review. [Recovery standard]
- The prototype's single-process lock prevents local races only. In-memory counters, token records, session versions and sinks disappear on restart and diverge across workers; they do not provide durable rate limiting, cross-instance session invalidation, delivery, audit history, abuse protections, or production availability. No migration is needed for this prototype; production would require shared transactional persistence, durable owner delivery and monitored fail-closed behavior, plus privacy/retention and security review. These are **limitations**, not promised follow-up implementation. [Story; Recovery standard]
- Run locally and test with pytest and Flask test clients plus a fake clock; do **not** deploy or add CI/CD deployment workflows. A test review should verify two or more pre-reset sessions lose access, a different account retains access, repeated success records one notification per success, and no notification is added for failed/replayed/expired changes. Verify response parity including fifth/sixth attempts, under/over limit and existing/nonexistent synthetic addresses; compare status, redirect, rendered content and account-dependent headers/cookies. Cover one instant before expiry, exact expiry, after expiry and the rolling-hour boundary. [Story; Recovery standard]

## Significant decisions and alternatives

| Decision | Alternative considered | Reason and limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-process synchronized, injectable state and clock | SQL database, distributed cache or external queue | Matches synthetic in-memory scope and enables deterministic race/boundary tests. No durability or cross-worker claims. |
| Rolling 3600-second window per normalized identifier, with silent suppression after five | Calendar-hour bucket or visible `429` | Defines a precise testable interpretation of “per hour”; silent, same-response throttling preserves ACC-STD-01 parity. Accounting nonexistent keys too is a privacy-preserving design choice, not a sourced mandate. |
| Opaque random reset token, digest-only index, inspectable in-memory owner outbox | Expose link in confirmation, use external email or self-contained signed URL | Exercises links without external service or public account disclosure; outbox holding URLs remains sensitive prototype data. |
| Per-account session-version guard on every authenticated request | Keep only a browser-local logout or enumerate server-side session IDs | Covers every previously active Flask cookie for the account, including other clients, while remaining process-local; guards must not be bypassed. |
| Commit-time strict `now < expires_at` and lock-protected one-use transition | Check only when link page is opened or consume on GET | Meets exact 30-minute boundary, prevents replay and avoids consuming a link by a preview/prefetch. |
| Minimal synthetic sign-in and proposed recovery templates | Infer a complete login policy or assert the recovery screens were pictured | Makes all-session sign-out observable without overclaiming the sole wireframe. |
| Synchronous in-memory notification on each committed reset | Fire-and-forget or real mail delivery | Enables one record per successful reset in a small prototype; no durable delivery guarantee. |

## Explicit assumptions and open questions

- **Assumptions for this design only:** synthetic fixture addresses can be normalized consistently; a minimal synthetic sign-in can be used to exercise invalidation; a process-local test outbox can convey links; a simple nonempty-password validation rule is sufficient until a password policy is specified. None is evidenced by the image or a production standard beyond the cited reset constraints.
- **Confirm before implementation:** Must the sign-in button authenticate synthetic accounts, or may sessions be test-established? Are `name@example.com` and `********` literal placeholders rather than values, and what responsive fidelity is expected? Should owner-directed reset links be available only to tests or to a local demonstration viewer? Is a rolling window and accounting nonexistent keys acceptable? What exact password policy and recovery-page copy should be adopted? Is the owner-notification record sufficient for the in-memory sink, without real delivery? These questions do not alter the exact ACC-STD-01/02/03 obligations.
